notes:
I've put together notes for all twelve verses, but there are real gaps. My search and fetch budget ran out before I could reach any Lutheran, Pentecostal or Orthodox source, or any page on prosperity or word-of-faith teaching. I also found nothing from bibleodyssey.org and only one translation note from netbible.org. The Enduring Word page cut off partway through verse 10, and Augustine's exposition (newadvent.org) cut off at verse 4. Where those sections are missing, I've left them out. Several "traditions differ" points below come from older commentators labelled by tradition on StudyLight, not from current denominational sites.

---

**Title / v. 1**
- **Gittith:** The study notes say it is probably a musical or liturgical term; here and in Psalms 8 and 81, possibly brought from Gath by David. https://biblehub.com/psalms/84.htm. Spurgeon notes that it is said to mean "wine press." He says the joy of God's house is sweeter than the joy of the wine press. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps084.cfm
- **Sons of Korah:** Guzik says they were Levites descended from Kohath who served in temple music. Their ancestor Korah rebelled and died, but his sons were spared. Perhaps they were so grateful for this mercy that they became notable in Israel for praising God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-84/
- **Who wrote it:** Calvin thinks it was probably David, written while he was an exile. https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_psalms_volume_3/psalm_84.htm. Matthew Henry suggests it was written when Absalom's rebellion drove David out of Jerusalem. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_084.cfm
- **"How lovely":** Guzik quotes Kidner: the phrase means "how dear," and it is the language of love poetry. He also quotes Spurgeon's view that the psalmist doesn't say *how* lovely because his feelings couldn't be put into words. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-84/
- **Catholic reading:** The Greek and Latin title reads "for the winepresses." Augustine takes the winepresses to be the Church in this life. Believers are "pressed" by trouble so that they become wine and are stored in God's cellar. He says the singer is the Body of Christ. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801084.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik says the house mattered to the psalmist because he met God there. He quotes Spurgeon: the psalmist loved the house because he loved the God of the house. Guzik also warns church leaders and worshippers to look for meeting "the living God," not programmes or entertainment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-84/
- Spurgeon's notes say the Hebrew word for "faints" means to be consumed with longing, like someone "dying of love." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps084.cfm
- **Catholic reading:** Augustine reads the verse in two parts. The longing is the groan in the winepress. The Latin "my heart and my flesh have rejoiced" is hope holding on. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801084.htm

**v. 3**
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik quotes Boice: the sparrow stands for the insignificant and the swallow for the restless, and both find a place near God's altar. He also quotes Spurgeon on the double "my King and my God" as holding on to God with both hands. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-84/
- Spurgeon pictures the free birds coming right up to the altars, which David, far away, envied. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps084.cfm
- **Catholic reading:** Augustine makes the sparrow the heart and the dove the flesh. The "nest" where the dove lays her young (good works) is the altar, meaning the Church's faith. Good works done outside the Church are like young laid outside the nest. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801084.htm. Haydock defends the Latin "turtle-dove" against the modern "swallow." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/psalms-83.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik says the psalmist moves from envying the birds to envying the priests who lived at God's house. He quotes Baker: praising God *still*, without stopping, is "a busy work." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-84/
- **Catholic reading:** Augustine applies the verse to the heavenly Jerusalem. There, with no more need for works of mercy, the whole duty will be "an unceasing Hallelujah." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801084.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik says the person whose strength is in God sees himself as a pilgrim in this world. Loving God's house prepares him for life in the world; it is not an escape from it. He quotes Kidner: "If he cannot be at Zion, he can be with God; if he cannot enjoy sweetness he can find strength." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-84/
- **Catholic reading:** Augustine reads the Latin "he has placed steps in his heart." God's grace sets "upward steps" in the heart, because a weak body cannot fly to blessedness by itself. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801084.htm

**v. 6** (the most discussed verse)
- **Meaning of "Baca":** Guzik says the meaning is uncertain, either weeping or drought, but both suggest trouble. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-84/. Ellicott notes that the ancient versions all have "valley of weeping." Through the Latin *vallis lacrymosa* this became Europe's religious phrase for life itself. https://biblehub.com/psalms/84-6.htm. The Cambridge Bible says the word probably means a balsam tree. Its point is that faith turns it into a place of springs, finding refreshment under the most untoward circumstances, while God refreshes them with showers of blessing from above. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/84-6.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** When the righteous suffer, they turn the time into refreshment. The rain is God's grace, which makes them grow in righteousness and true holiness. https://biblehub.com/psalms/84-6.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The pilgrims' faith brings water out of the desert, and God also sends rain from above. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/84-6.htm
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** He describes it as a dry pass where pits were dug to hold rainwater. He applies it to Christ going with his people through this "vale of tears." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/84-6.html
- **Clarke (Methodist):** He links Baca with Bochim, "the Valley of Weeping," in Judges 2. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/84-6.html
- **Constable:** He takes it as a picture of being spiritually dry. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/84-6.html
- **Luther's reading:** The Cambridge Bible notes that Jerome rendered the end of the verse "the teacher shall be clothed with blessing," and a rendering followed by Luther. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/84-6.htm
- **Catholic reading:** For Augustine the valley of weeping is the winepress, and pious tears in trouble are the new wine of those that love. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801084.htm

**v. 7**
- Guzik says ordinary travellers go from strength to tiredness, but these pilgrims go from strength to strength. He quotes Clarke (Methodist): they go "from one degree of grace to another." He also quotes Spurgeon: the goal is to appear *before God*, not just to be in the gathering. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-84/
- **Philpot (Strict Baptist, Calvinist):** He reads the verse as a promise that no true pilgrim will die in the valley. "Every one" reaches Zion. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jcp/psalms-84.html

**v. 8**
- Guzik says the psalm becomes a prayer. Calling on "the God of Jacob" rests the request on God's long faithfulness to his covenant people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-84/
- Matthew Henry notes the titles used: God of hosts (all power), God of Jacob (in covenant with his people). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_084.cfm

**v. 9** (real disagreement)
- **Is "our shield" God or the king?** The Cambridge Bible allows both readings but prefers the king. The parallel with "your anointed" supports this, and Psalm 89:18 calls the king "our shield." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/84-9.htm. Keil & Delitzsch argue from the word order that "our shield" is God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/84-9.htm. Coffman strongly rejects the king reading and points to verse 11. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/84-9.html. Guzik takes "shield" as Israel's literal defence and "anointed" as the king. He says the anointed points first to David or Solomon and ultimately to the Messiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-84/
- **Is "anointed" Christ?** The commentators differ:
  - Barnes (Presbyterian) says the allusion here is not to Christ. He says the verse does not support the common prayer that God would see us in the face of his anointed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/84-9.htm
  - Gill (Baptist) prefers the Messiah reading. God is asked to look on Christ's righteousness, blood and sacrifice for the psalmist's sake. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/psalms/84-9.html
  - Clarke (Methodist) reads it as the Mediator, Christ, but notes that others apply it to David, Zerubbabel or Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/84-9.html
  - Matthew Henry and the Geneva notes read it as "for Christ's sake." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/84-9.htm
  - The Pulpit homilies apply "anointed" to believers set apart for God's service. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/84-9.htm
- **Catholic text:** The Douay-Rheims reads "look on the face of thy Christ." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/psalms/84-9.html

**v. 10**
- Guzik compares the verse to Paul's "all things but loss." He quotes Morgan: the choice isn't heroic, just common sense. He also quotes Spurgeon: "God's worst is better than the devil's best." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-84/
- **"Doorkeeper":** Spurgeon's notes point out that the Korahites really were temple gatekeepers. They also note the Hebrew margin: "sit at the threshold." https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps084.php. Clarke also notes that the Korahites were gatekeepers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/84-1.html
- Keil & Delitzsch observe that the psalm says "tents," not "palaces," of the wicked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/84-9.htm

**v. 11** (traditions differ in emphasis)
- **"Sun":** Keil & Delitzsch say this is the only place where God is directly called a sun. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/84-11.htm. Barnes and Clarke note that the Greek and Latin versions read instead "the Lord loves mercy and truth." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/84-11.html. The NET Bible renders the line "For the LORD God is our sovereign protector." https://biblehub.com/parallel/psalms/84-11.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** God's kindly face gives his people life. The verse teaches that whatever excellence may be in us proceeds solely from the grace of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/84-11.html
- **Clarke (Methodist/Arminian):** Grace pardons and *purifies*, and then glory is given to the *sanctified*. He warns that sinners and hypocrites need not expect these blessings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/84-11.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Grace prepares for glory, and glory perfects grace. Both are God's free gift. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_084.cfm
- **"No good thing":** Poole and Benson say this means what is *truly* good for the believer. They suggest David added it because his own troubles came from his own failures, not from any lack in God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/84-11.htm. A Pulpit homily calls it a carefully qualified promise: it says "no *good* thing," and only God decides what is good. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/84-11.htm. The Bible Hub study notes say integrity means wholehearted loyalty, not sinless perfection. They also say material abundance is not guaranteed. https://biblehub.com/psalms/84-11.htm. This is the nearest I found to a response to prosperity readings, but it doesn't name any movement.

**v. 12**
- Bible Hub's summary says the psalm ends by repeating its theme: the one who trusts the LORD of Hosts is truly blessed. https://biblehub.com/psalms/84.htm
- Clarke ties the verse to verse 11: since God gives all these gifts, the psalmist was right to call the one who trusts him blessed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/84-11.html
- Matthew Henry: whatever his circumstances, the one who trusts the Lord of hosts is truly happy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/84-9.htm
